subtopics.title: Classify quantitative data
subtopics.exposition: Data refers to the pieces of information that have been observed and recorded, from an experiment or a survey. Quantitative data are data that can be written as numbers. Discrete quantitative data can be represented by integers and usually occur when we count things. Examples of discrete quantitative data given in the book are the number of learners in a class, the number of molecules in a chemical solution, and the number of SMS messages sent in one day. Continuous quantitative data can be represented by real numbers. Examples of continuous quantitative data given in the book are the height or mass of a person, the distance travelled by a car, and the duration of a phone call. There are two main types of data: quantitative and qualitative. Quantitative data can be discrete or continuous. A table of counts, such as how many times each colour appears, is a discrete quantitative data set because each count is an integer. To classify a data set as quantitative and discrete, check whether it is a count represented by integers: a count represented by an integer is quantitative and discrete (the number of SMS messages sent the previous day by each of 20 classmates is an example).

subtopics.title: Classify qualitative data
subtopics.exposition: Qualitative data are data that cannot be written as numbers. Categorical data can come from one of a limited number of possibilities. Examples of categorical data given in the book are your favourite cooldrink, the colour of your cell phone, and the language that you learnt to speak at home. Anecdotal data take the form of an interview or a story. An example of anecdotal data given in the book is asking someone what their personal experience was when using a product. Two common types of qualitative data are categorical data and anecdotal data. Categorical qualitative data are sometimes turned into quantitative data by counting the number of times that each category appears. To classify a data set as categorical qualitative data, check whether each response comes from one of a small number of possibilities (for example, a small number of possible colours). The same data can be represented in a different way by counting how many times each category (for example, each colour) appears. To classify a data set as qualitative and categorical, check that each response is not a number but one of a small number of possibilities (for example, which cellular provider a learner uses).

claims.claim: Data refers to the pieces of information that have been observed and recorded, from an experiment or a survey.
The word data is the plural of the word datum, so one should say "the data are" and not "the data is".
There are two main types of data: quantitative and qualitative.

Quantitative data can be discrete or continuous.

A table of counts, such as how many times each colour appears, is a discrete quantitative data set because each count is an integer.

Categorical data can come from one of a limited number of possibilities.
Examples of categorical data given in the book are your favourite cooldrink, the colour of your cell phone, and the language that you learnt to speak at home.

To classify a data set as qualitative and categorical, check that each response is not a number but one of a small number of possibilities (for example, which cellular provider a learner uses).
